items.title: The Sociological Imagination
items.description: In this session, you will learn C. Wright Mills' concept of the 'sociological imagination,' which distinguishes between 'personal troubles' and 'public issues.' By the end, you will be able to connect your private biography with historical and social structures. This foundational concept is essential for your course project, as it provides the lens through which you will analyze your own life path.

items.title: Structure and Agency
items.description: This session explores the tension between agency—your power to act independently—and social structure—the organized patterns of relationships that limit your choices. You will understand how society both constrains and enables human action. Mastering this balance is key to moving beyond a purely individualistic worldview toward a sophisticated sociological analysis.

items.title: Social Facts
items.description: This session introduces Émile Durkheim’s 'social facts,' which are ways of acting and thinking external to the individual that exert social control. You will learn to identify these invisible forces, such as laws, morals, and customs, that shape collective behavior. This helps you develop the critical awareness needed to see society as a distinct reality worthy of scientific study.

items.title: Sociology and Everyday Life
items.description: This session applies the sociological perspective to mundane activities, showing how even the most private acts are socially patterned. You will learn to 'make the familiar strange' by questioning things you usually take for granted. This develops your ability to conduct applied analysis on your own daily routines, a core skill for the later units on culture and institutions.

items.title: Functionalism
items.description: You will examine the functionalist perspective, which views society as a complex system of interrelated parts working together to promote solidarity and stability. You will learn about manifest and latent functions, as well as social dysfunctions. This helps you understand the 'macro' logic of how social order is maintained across time.

items.title: Conflict Theory
items.description: This session covers the conflict perspective, rooted in the work of Karl Marx, which focuses on power, inequality, and social struggle. You will learn how social structures often benefit some groups at the expense of others. This is a crucial foundation for Unit 3, where we will dive deeper into racial and gender-based inequality.

items.title: Symbolic Interactionism
items.description: You will explore the micro-level perspective of symbolic interactionism, focusing on how individuals create meaning through social interaction. You will learn how symbols—words, gestures, and objects—shape our shared reality. This session transitions the course toward the study of the self and identity in Unit 2.

items.title: Contemporary Theories
items.description: This session introduces modern developments such as Feminist Theory and Postmodernism, which challenge and expand traditional perspectives. You will learn how these theories address modern complexities like intersectionality and the decline of 'grand narratives.' This ensures your sociological master-toolkit is up-to-date for contemporary social issues.

items.title: Surveys and Sampling
items.description: You will learn the mechanics of quantitative research, specifically how to design surveys and select representative samples from populations. You will understand why random sampling is necessary to generalize results to a larger group. This knowledge is fundamental for becoming a critical consumer of social statistics and media reports.

items.title: Experiments and Field Research
items.description: This session compares the controlled environment of laboratory experiments with the naturalistic setting of field research. You will learn how sociologists test hypotheses and observe social behavior in real-time. This helps you understand the trade-offs between 'control' and 'authenticity' in social science.

items.title: Ethnography and Interviews
items.description: You will learn about qualitative methods like ethnography (participant observation) and in-depth interviews, which prioritize 'thick description' and the participant's point of view. You will understand how these methods uncover the 'why' behind social patterns. This session emphasizes the 'human' side of data collection often missing from statistics.

items.title: Measurement, Causality, and Ethics
items.description: This session covers the rigorous requirements of research: operationalizing variables, distinguishing correlation from causation, and adhering to institutional review board (IRB) ethics. You will learn why sociologists must protect human subjects and avoid harm. This ensures you understand sociology not just as a set of ideas, but as an ethical and disciplined science.

items.title: Research Question and Methodology Design
items.description: Define a specific social group or community to study and select the appropriate research methods (ethnography, survey, or interview) to investigate a specific social phenomenon within that group.

items.title: The Sociological Perspective Comprehensive Exam
items.description: Verify the learner's ability to apply the sociological imagination, distinguish between major theoretical paradigms, and evaluate the appropriateness of various research methods for specific social questions.

items.title: Norms and Values
items.description: This session introduces the distinction between values—the abstract ideals of a society—and norms—the specific rules of conduct that implement those values. You will learn to identify folkways, mores, and taboos, gaining the ability to analyze how social order is maintained through informal and formal sanctions. This builds the foundational vocabulary needed to understand why people conform to social expectations in their daily lives.

items.title: Symbols and Language
items.description: This session examines language as the primary vehicle of culture and the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, which suggests language shapes our perception of reality. You will understand how symbols carry shared meanings and how linguistic shifts reflect social change. This is critical for recognizing how our very thoughts are structured by the cultural tools available to us.

items.title: Subcultures and Countercultures
items.description: This session distinguishes between subcultures, which exist within the dominant culture, and countercultures, which actively reject it. You will learn to identify the social functions of these groups and how they contribute to social diversity or conflict. This allows you to look past a monolithic view of 'society' and see the vibrant, often conflicting layers of group life.

items.title: Cultural Capital and Change
items.description: This session introduces Pierre Bourdieu's concept of cultural capital and the processes of cultural lag and diffusion. You will understand how cultural knowledge can function as a form of currency that reinforces social class and how technology drives rapid cultural shifts. This links cultural themes to the broader structures of inequality that will be explored in the next unit.

items.title: Agents of Socialization
items.description: This session identifies the primary groups and institutions—family, school, peers, and mass media—that transmit culture to the individual. You will learn how these agents often provide conflicting messages and how they shape our initial worldviews. Understanding these agents is essential for mapping the 'sociological autobiography' of your own life.

items.title: Socialization Across the Life Course
items.description: This session moves beyond childhood to explore how socialization continues through adolescence, adulthood, and old age. You will examine the concept of 'anticipatory socialization' and 'resocialization' in total institutions. This helps you realize that the 'self' is not a finished product but a continuous social project.

items.title: Roles and Identity
items.description: This session defines statuses (ascribed and achieved) and roles, focusing on role conflict and role strain. You will learn how the positions we occupy in society dictate the behaviors expected of us. Mastering these concepts allows you to analyze the structural pressures that cause personal stress in daily life.

items.title: The Presentation of Self
items.description: Using Erving Goffman’s dramaturgical analysis, this session explores the 'front stage' and 'back stage' of social life and the practice of impression management. You will gain a framework for understanding how we perform our identities to others, particularly in the context of social media. This session bridges the gap between individual psychology and social structure.

items.title: Cultural and Socialization Field Notes
items.description: Conduct initial observations or interviews to identify the core values, norms, and agents of socialization that shape identity within your chosen community.

items.title: Primary and Secondary Groups
items.description: This session distinguishes between intimate, long-term primary groups and impersonal, goal-oriented secondary groups. You will learn how the shift from Gemeinschaft (community) to Gesellschaft (society) characterizes modern life. This provides the context for understanding where individuals find emotional support versus instrumental resources.

items.title: Organizations and Bureaucracy
items.description: This session analyzes the characteristics of ideal-typical bureaucracies as defined by Max Weber and the 'McDonaldization' of society. You will understand the efficiency and the 'iron cage' of rationality that governs modern institutions. This is vital for navigating and critiquing the organizations you deal with daily, from universities to corporations.

items.title: Social Networks
items.description: This session introduces social network analysis and the concept of 'the strength of weak ties' by Mark Granovetter. You will learn how information and opportunities flow through social ties that aren't necessarily close friendships. This changes your perspective on networking from a 'sleazy' activity to a structural necessity for social mobility.

items.title: Social Capital
items.description: This session explores social capital—the resources inherent in social relations that facilitate collective action. You will learn the difference between bonding and bridging social capital and how access to these resources varies by social class. This connects the study of groups to the larger questions of power and inequality that Unit 3 will address.

items.title: Culture and the Self Comprehensive Exam
items.description: Evaluate the student's ability to apply micro-sociological theories to identity formation, cultural transmission, and group dynamics.

items.title: Systems of Stratification
items.description: This session introduces the fundamental concepts of social stratification, comparing slavery, caste, and class systems across history and geography. You will learn to identify the varying degrees of social closure and ascription that define different societal hierarchies. This understanding provides the necessary baseline for analyzing why some social positions are inherently more advantageous than others in any given structure.

items.title: Class in Modern Societies
items.description: We will explore how sociologists define 'class' using the lenses of Marx's relationship to the means of production and Weber's multidimensional approach of property, power, and prestige. You will gain the ability to differentiate between economic wealth and social influence, allowing you to master the analytical tools required to map out the modern social hierarchy beyond simple income brackets.

items.title: Social Mobility
items.description: This session focuses on the movement of individuals or groups within the hierarchical system, specifically focusing on intergenerational and intragenerational mobility. You will be able to evaluate the extent to which modern societies are meritocratic versus how much they are governed by structural inheritance. This analysis is critical for assessing the 'American Dream' and similar cultural narratives through a rigorous sociological lens.

items.title: Poverty and Life Chances
items.description: We will analyze the distinction between absolute and relative poverty and how these conditions impact 'life chances' such as health, education, and longevity. You will understand how social class functions as a predictor of individual outcomes, moving the conversation from personal failing to structural disadvantage. This session directly connects the abstract concepts of stratification to the tangible realities of survival and well-being.

items.title: The Social Construction of Race
items.description: This session clarifies that race is a socio-political construct rather than a biological reality, examining how racial categories change over time and place. You will learn to recognize the process of 'racialization' and how societies create and maintain boundaries between groups. This builds the foundational understanding that racial inequality is a product of social decisions rather than natural differences.

items.title: Prejudice and Discrimination
items.description: We will distinguish between individual attitudes (prejudice) and actual behaviors (discrimination), and introduce the concept of implicit bias. You will gain a clear vocabulary for identifying different levels of social exclusion and the psychological mechanisms that sustain them. This is essential for understanding how social tension is maintained even in the absence of overt, legalized bigotry.

items.title: Segregation
items.description: This session examines the physical and social separation of categories of people, focusing on residential and educational segregation. You will analyze how historic policies and modern practices result in disparate environments for different racial groups. Understanding segregation is key to explaining why certain populations lack access to the resources and networks discussed in earlier units.

items.title: Structural Inequality
items.description: We synthesize the previous sessions to look at how racial inequality is reproduced through the legal, economic, and political systems without needing individual actors to be 'racist.' You will be able to explain the concept of systemic racism and its cumulative effects over generations. This session equips you to move beyond individual-level explanations to structural-level critiques of social justice.

items.title: Gender as a Social Structure
items.description: This session challenges the biological binary by presenting gender as a complex social institution that organizes every aspect of social life. You will learn the difference between sex and gender and understand the concept of 'doing gender' in everyday interaction. This provides the framework to see gender not as something people 'are' but as something they 'do' within a structured system.

items.title: Gender Socialization
items.description: We will examine how agents like family, peers, and media teach individuals the 'correct' way to be masculine or feminine. You will be able to identify the subtle and overt ways gender roles are reinforced from birth through adulthood. This session helps you understand how individual preferences are often shaped by societal expectations before we are even aware of them.

items.title: Work, Family, and the Gender Gap
items.description: This session focuses on the economic and domestic manifestations of gender inequality, including the wage gap and the 'second shift.' You will analyze how the division of labor in the home and the workplace reinforces the status of women and men differently. This session provides a bridge to Unit 4 by showing how gender inequality is operationalized within the institution of the family and the economy.

items.title: Sexuality and Society
items.description: We will explore how societies regulate sexual behavior and how sexual identities are socially constructed and politicized. You will learn about heteronormativity and the social hierarchies that privilege certain types of sexual orientations over others. This session concludes the unit by demonstrating that even our most intimate desires are filtered through and governed by social structures.

items.title: Social Inequality Mapping
items.description: Analyze how class, race, and gender dynamics create hierarchies or barriers within your community, using the theoretical frameworks of stratification.

items.title: Inequality and Stratification Exam
items.description: To evaluate the learner's ability to apply sociological theories of class, race, and gender to real-world scenarios and structural data.

items.title: Family Forms
items.description: This session explores the diverse structures of family across cultures and history, ranging from nuclear to extended and blended families. You will learn to identify different kinship patterns and understand how these forms adapt to economic and social pressures. Understanding family diversity is a prerequisite for analyzing how modern social policies impact different household types.

items.title: Family Change
items.description: This session examines the shifting dynamics of family life, including rising divorce rates, cohabitation, and delayed marriage. You will gain an understanding of the sociological drivers behind these trends and how they reflect broader shifts in gender roles and individual autonomy. This knowledge helps you evaluate the 'crisis of the family' narrative through an objective sociological lens.

items.title: Schooling and Credentials
items.description: This session investigates the transition from education as learning to education as a system of credentialing. You will learn about 'credential inflation' and the functionalist versus conflict perspectives on why we stay in school longer. This session clarifies how degrees serve as gatekeepers in the modern labor market.

items.title: Education and the Reproduction of Inequality
items.description: This session covers the 'hidden curriculum' and how schools often reinforce existing social hierarchies rather than providing a level playing field. You will be able to analyze how cultural capital and school funding mechanisms contribute to social reproduction. This is vital for understanding why educational attainment remains so closely tied to parental socioeconomic status.

items.title: Institutional Impact Analysis
items.description: Evaluate how major institutions like family or education systems support or constrain the individuals within your community.

items.title: Labor Markets
items.description: This session introduces the concept of primary and secondary labor markets and the sociological factors that determine job quality. You will learn how social networks and structural barriers segment the workforce into 'good' and 'bad' jobs. This provides the foundation for understanding systemic disparities in employment outcomes.

items.title: The Changing Workplace
items.description: This session discusses the shift from Fordism to post-Fordism, including the rise of the gig economy and precarious work. You will understand how automation and flexible specialization have transformed the daily experience of the worker. This session connects economic theory to the lived reality of contemporary professional life.

items.title: Consumption
items.description: This session moves from production to consumption, examining how what we buy defines who we are in a consumer society. You will learn about 'conspicuous consumption' and how lifestyle choices act as markers of social class. Understanding consumption is key to grasping how modern identity is constructed through the market.

items.title: Capitalism and Globalization
items.description: This session looks at the macro-economic structure of global capitalism and the international division of labor. You will explore World Systems Theory and how the global economy links the prosperity of core nations to the labor of peripheral nations. This completes your understanding of how local institutions are nested within global economic forces.

items.title: Religion and Society
items.description: This session defines religion as a social institution and examines its role in providing social cohesion and meaning. You will learn Durkheim’s concepts of the 'sacred' and the 'profane' and how collective effervescence builds community. This helps you look past individual faith to see religion’s structural function in society.

items.title: Secularization
items.description: This session investigates the secularization thesis and the counter-arguments regarding the persistence of religious belief in the modern world. You will analyze how modernization affects religious authority and the rise of 'spiritual but not religious' identities. This session prepares you to discuss the role of faith in a scientific and pluralistic age.

items.title: Media and Technology
items.description: This session analyzes the media as a 'fourth estate' and a tool for social construction. You will learn about media concentration, the digital divide, and how algorithms shape our perception of social reality. This knowledge is crucial for navigating the modern information landscape as a critical citizen.

items.title: Health Disparities
items.description: This session explores the social determinants of health and the 'medicalization' of social problems. You will learn why life expectancy and health outcomes vary so significantly by class, race, and geography. This session bridges the gap between individual biology and the structural 'causes of the causes' of illness.

items.title: Institutions Unit Exam
items.description: Evaluate the student's ability to analyze how social institutions like family, education, economy, religion, media, and healthcare interact to organize society and reproduce inequality.

items.title: Defining Deviance
items.description: This session introduces deviance not as an inherent quality of an act, but as a social construction that varies across time and space. You will learn to differentiate between formal and informal deviance and understand the concept of social control. This foundational perspective is essential for your goal of critical awareness, as it challenges the 'common sense' view of right and wrong by showing how definitions of deviance serve social functions.

items.title: Theories of Deviance
items.description: We will explore why deviance occurs through the lenses of Strain Theory, Labeling Theory, and Control Theory. You will gain the ability to analyze deviant behavior using different theoretical frameworks, moving beyond individual pathology to social explanation. This session provides the analytical tools required for the academic mastery of sociological thought, bridging the gap between individual actions and structural pressures.

items.title: Crime
items.description: This session examines the sociological study of crime, focusing on how crime is measured and the different categories of criminal activity. You will learn about the limitations of official crime statistics and the social profile of offenders and victims. Understanding these patterns is crucial for an applied analysis of public policy and helps you see how social inequality, studied in Unit 3, manifests in the criminal justice system.

items.title: Punishment and the Justice System
items.description: We will analyze the functions of punishment, including retribution, deterrence, rehabilitation, and societal protection, alongside the rise of mass incarceration. You will be able to critically evaluate the effectiveness of different correctional philosophies and the systemic biases within the legal system. This connects directly to your goal of understanding how social structures shape lives, specifically through the state's power to label and confine.

items.title: Demography
items.description: You will learn the basic tools of demographic analysis, including fertility, mortality, and migration rates, and the Demographic Transition Model. This session enables you to predict how changes in population structure influence social institutions like the economy and healthcare. It provides the essential data-driven foundation for understanding the 'big picture' of social change.

items.title: Migration
items.description: This session explores the push and pull factors of human movement and the social consequences of global migration patterns. You will understand how migration reshapes culture, labor markets, and national identities. This is a key component of your applied analysis goal, as migration is one of the most significant drivers of contemporary social transformation.

items.title: Aging Societies
items.description: We examine the sociological implications of the 'graying' of the world, focusing on the social construction of age and the challenges of aging populations. You will learn to analyze how different societies distribute resources and care for older generations. This session prepares you to understand future institutional shifts in family and health, as discussed in Unit 4.

items.title: Urbanization and Community
items.description: This session covers the growth of cities and the shift from rural community life to urban social structures. You will explore concepts like 'urbanism as a way of life' and the development of suburbs and gentrification. This knowledge allows you to analyze how physical space and geographic location influence social interaction and inequality.

items.title: Social Movements
items.description: You will learn how social movements are organized and why people join them, focusing on Resource Mobilization and Frame Analysis. This session provides the conceptual framework to understand how marginalized groups exert agency to change social structures. This is central to your project work, as it illustrates the active side of the sociological imagination.

items.title: Collective Action
items.description: This session looks at less organized forms of social change, such as crowds, riots, and fads, and the theories that explain them. You will understand the dynamics of 'emergent norms' and how individual behavior changes in collective settings. This rounds out your understanding of how social order can temporarily break down and lead to new social forms.

items.title: Technology and Social Change
items.description: We will analyze how technological innovations—from the steam engine to the internet—act as catalysts for social reorganization. You will learn to evaluate the 'cultural lag' that occurs when material culture outpaces non-material culture. This session is vital for understanding the 'future of society' component of your learning goals, particularly regarding globalization.

items.title: Environment and the Future of Society
items.description: In our final session, we explore the relationship between human society and the natural environment, focusing on environmental sociology and sustainability. You will gain a macro-level perspective on how social systems must adapt to environmental constraints. This synthesizes everything you have learned about institutions, inequality, and change into a cohesive view of the challenges facing 21st-century society.

items.title: Social Change Proposal and Final Synthesis
items.description: Identify a 'deviant' behavior or social problem in the group and design a social movement or policy intervention strategy to address it, then compile all previous parts into the final report.

items.title: Deviance and Social Change Comprehensive Exam
items.description: Evaluate the learner's ability to synthesize theories of social control, demographic shifts, and the mechanisms of collective action and social change.

You will understand how social class functions as a predictor of individual outcomes, moving the conversation from personal failing to structural disadvantage. This session directly connects the abstract concepts of stratification to the tangible realities of survival and well-being.

input.title: The Social Construction of Race
input.description: This session clarifies that race is a socio-political construct rather than a biological reality, examining how racial categories change over time and place. You will learn to recognize the process of 'racialization' and how societies create and maintain boundaries between groups. This builds the foundational understanding that racial inequality is a product of social decisions rather than natural differences.

input.title: Prejudice and Discrimination
input.description: We will distinguish between individual attitudes (prejudice) and actual behaviors (discrimination), and introduce the concept of implicit bias. You will gain a clear vocabulary for identifying different levels of social exclusion and the psychological mechanisms that sustain them. This is essential for understanding how social tension is maintained even in the absence of overt, legalized bigotry.

input.title: Segregation
input.description: This session examines the physical and social separation of categories of people, focusing on residential and educational segregation. You will analyze how historic policies and modern practices result in disparate environments for different racial groups. Understanding segregation is key to explaining why certain populations lack access to the resources and networks discussed in earlier units.

input.title: Structural Inequality
input.description: We synthesize the previous sessions to look at how racial inequality is reproduced through the legal, economic, and political systems without needing individual actors to be 'racist.' You will be able to explain the concept of systemic racism and its cumulative effects over generations. This session equips you to move beyond individual-level explanations to structural-level critiques of social justice.

input.title: Gender as a Social Structure
input.description: This session challenges the biological binary by presenting gender as a complex social institution that organizes every aspect of social life. You will learn the difference between sex and gender and understand the concept of 'doing gender' in everyday interaction. This provides the framework to see gender not as something people 'are' but as something they 'do' within a structured system.

input.title: Gender Socialization
input.description: We will examine how agents like family, peers, and media teach individuals the 'correct' way to be masculine or feminine. You will be able to identify the subtle and overt ways gender roles are reinforced from birth through adulthood. This session helps you understand how individual preferences are often shaped by societal expectations before we are even aware of them.

input.title: Work, Family, and the Gender Gap
input.description: This session focuses on the economic and domestic manifestations of gender inequality, including the wage gap and the 'second shift.' You will analyze how the division of labor in the home and the workplace reinforces the status of women and men differently. This session provides a bridge to Unit 4 by showing how gender inequality is operationalized within the institution of the family and the economy.

input.title: Sexuality and Society
input.description: We will explore how societies regulate sexual behavior and how sexual identities are socially constructed and politicized. You will learn about heteronormativity and the social hierarchies that privilege certain types of sexual orientations over others. This session concludes the unit by demonstrating that even our most intimate desires are filtered through and governed by social structures.

input.title: Social Inequality Mapping
input.description: Analyze how class, race, and gender dynamics create hierarchies or barriers within your community, using the theoretical frameworks of stratification.

input.title: Inequality and Stratification Exam
input.description: To evaluate the learner's ability to apply sociological theories of class, race, and gender to real-world scenarios and structural data.

input.title: Family Forms
input.description: This session explores the diverse structures of family across cultures and history, ranging from nuclear to extended and blended families. You will learn to identify different kinship patterns and understand how these forms adapt to economic and social pressures. Understanding family diversity is a prerequisite for analyzing how modern social policies impact different household types.

input.title: Family Change
input.description: This session examines the shifting dynamics of family life, including rising divorce rates, cohabitation, and delayed marriage. You will gain an understanding of the sociological drivers behind these trends and how they reflect broader shifts in gender roles and individual autonomy. This knowledge helps you evaluate the 'crisis of the family' narrative through an objective sociological lens.

input.title: Schooling and Credentials
input.description: This session investigates the transition from education as learning to education as a system of credentialing. You will learn about 'credential inflation' and the functionalist versus conflict perspectives on why we stay in school longer. This session clarifies how degrees serve as gatekeepers in the modern labor market.

input.title: Education and the Reproduction of Inequality
input.description: This session covers the 'hidden curriculum' and how schools often reinforce existing social hierarchies rather than providing a level playing field. You will be able to analyze how cultural capital and school funding mechanisms contribute to social reproduction. This is vital for understanding why educational attainment remains so closely tied to parental socioeconomic status.

input.title: Institutional Impact Analysis
input.description: Evaluate how major institutions like family or education systems support or constrain the individuals within your community.

input.title: Labor Markets
input.description: This session introduces the concept of primary and secondary labor markets and the sociological factors that determine job quality. You will learn how social networks and structural barriers segment the workforce into 'good' and 'bad' jobs. This provides the foundation for understanding systemic disparities in employment outcomes.

input.title: The Changing Workplace
input.description: This session discusses the shift from Fordism to post-Fordism, including the rise of the gig economy and precarious work. You will understand how automation and flexible specialization have transformed the daily experience of the worker. This session connects economic theory to the lived reality of contemporary professional life.

input.title: Consumption
input.description: This session moves from production to consumption, examining how what we buy defines who we are in a consumer society. You will learn about 'conspicuous consumption' and how lifestyle choices act as markers of social class. Understanding consumption is key to grasping how modern identity is constructed through the market.

input.title: Capitalism and Globalization
input.description: This session looks at the macro-economic structure of global capitalism and the international division of labor. You will explore World Systems Theory and how the global economy links the prosperity of core nations to the labor of peripheral nations. This completes your understanding of how local institutions are nested within global economic forces.

input.title: Religion and Society
input.description: This session defines religion as a social institution and examines its role in providing social cohesion and meaning. You will learn Durkheim’s concepts of the 'sacred' and the 'profane' and how collective effervescence builds community. This helps you look past individual faith to see religion’s structural function in society.

input.title: Secularization
input.description: This session investigates the secularization thesis and the counter-arguments regarding the persistence of religious belief in the modern world. You will analyze how modernization affects religious authority and the rise of 'spiritual but not religious' identities. This session prepares you to discuss the role of faith in a scientific and pluralistic age.

input.title: Media and Technology
input.description: This session analyzes the media as a 'fourth estate' and a tool for social construction. You will learn about media concentration, the digital divide, and how algorithms shape our perception of social reality. This knowledge is crucial for navigating the modern information landscape as a critical citizen.

input.title: Health Disparities
input.description: This session explores the social determinants of health and the 'medicalization' of social problems. You will learn why life expectancy and health outcomes vary so significantly by class, race, and geography. This session bridges the gap between individual biology and the structural 'causes of the causes' of illness.

input.title: Institutions Unit Exam
input.description: Evaluate the student's ability to analyze how social institutions like family, education, economy, religion, media, and healthcare interact to organize society and reproduce inequality.

input.title: Defining Deviance
input.description: This session introduces deviance not as an inherent quality of an act, but as a social construction that varies across time and space. You will learn to differentiate between formal and informal deviance and understand the concept of social control. This foundational perspective is essential for your goal of critical awareness, as it challenges the 'common sense' view of right and wrong by showing how definitions of deviance serve social functions.

input.title: Theories of Deviance
input.description: We will explore why deviance occurs through the lenses of Strain Theory, Labeling Theory, and Control Theory. You will gain the ability to analyze deviant behavior using different theoretical frameworks, moving beyond individual pathology to social explanation. This session provides the analytical tools required for the academic mastery of sociological thought, bridging the gap between individual actions and structural pressures.

input.title: Crime
input.description: This session examines the sociological study of crime, focusing on how crime is measured and the different categories of criminal activity. You will learn about the limitations of official crime statistics and the social profile of offenders and victims. Understanding these patterns is crucial for an applied analysis of public policy and helps you see how social inequality, studied in Unit 3, manifests in the criminal justice system.

input.title: Punishment and the Justice System
input.description: We will analyze the functions of punishment, including retribution, deterrence, rehabilitation, and societal protection, alongside the rise of mass incarceration. You will be able to critically evaluate the effectiveness of different correctional philosophies and the systemic biases within the legal system. This connects directly to your goal of understanding how social structures shape lives, specifically through the state's power to label and confine.

input.title: Demography
input.description: You will learn the basic tools of demographic analysis, including fertility, mortality, and migration rates, and the Demographic Transition Model. This session enables you to predict how changes in population structure influence social institutions like the economy and healthcare. It provides the essential data-driven foundation for understanding the 'big picture' of social change.

input.title: Migration
input.description: This session explores the push and pull factors of human movement and the social consequences of global migration patterns. You will understand how migration reshapes culture, labor markets, and national identities. This is a key component of your applied analysis goal, as migration is one of the most significant drivers of contemporary social transformation.

input.title: Aging Societies
input.description: We examine the sociological implications of the 'graying' of the world, focusing on the social construction of age and the challenges of aging populations. You will learn to analyze how different societies distribute resources and care for older generations. This session prepares you to understand future institutional shifts in family and health, as discussed in Unit 4.

input.title: Urbanization and Community
input.description: This session covers the growth of cities and the shift from rural community life to urban social structures. You will explore concepts like 'urbanism as a way of life' and the development of suburbs and gentrification. This knowledge allows you to analyze how physical space and geographic location influence social interaction and inequality.

input.title: Social Movements
input.description: You will learn how social movements are organized and why people join them, focusing on Resource Mobilization and Frame Analysis. This session provides the conceptual framework to understand how marginalized groups exert agency to change social structures. This is central to your project work, as it illustrates the active side of the sociological imagination.

input.title: Collective Action
input.description: This session looks at less organized forms of social change, such as crowds, riots, and fads, and the theories that explain them. You will understand the dynamics of 'emergent norms' and how individual behavior changes in collective settings. This rounds out your understanding of how social order can temporarily break down and lead to new social forms.

input.title: Technology and Social Change
input.description: We will analyze how technological innovations—from the steam engine to the internet—act as catalysts for social reorganization. You will learn to evaluate the 'cultural lag' that occurs when material culture outpaces non-material culture. This session is vital for understanding the 'future of society' component of your learning goals, particularly regarding globalization.

input.title: Environment and the Future of Society
input.description: In our final session, we explore the relationship between human society and the natural environment, focusing on environmental sociology and sustainability. You will gain a macro-level perspective on how social systems must adapt to environmental constraints. This synthesizes everything you have learned about institutions, inequality, and change into a cohesive view of the challenges facing 21st-century society.

input.title: Social Change Proposal and Final Synthesis
input.description: Identify a 'deviant' behavior or social problem in the group and design a social movement or policy intervention strategy to address it, then compile all previous parts into the final report.

input.title: Deviance and Social Change Comprehensive Exam
input.description: Evaluate the learner's ability to synthesize theories of social control, demographic shifts, and the mechanisms of collective action and social change.

tasks.title: Social Mobility
tasks.description: This session focuses on the movement of individuals or groups within the hierarchical system, specifically focusing on intergenerational and intragenerational mobility. You will be able to evaluate the extent to which modern societies are meritocratic versus how much they are governed by structural inheritance. This analysis is critical for assessing the 'American Dream' and similar cultural narratives through a rigorous sociological lens.

tasks.title: Class in Modern Societies
tasks.description: We will explore how sociologists define 'class' using the lenses of Marx's relationship to the means of production and Weber's multidimensional approach of property, power, and prestige. You will gain the ability to differentiate between economic wealth and social influence, allowing you to master the analytical tools required to map out the modern social hierarchy beyond simple income brackets.

tasks.title: Systems of Stratification
tasks.description: This session introduces the fundamental concepts of social stratification, comparing slavery, caste, and class systems across history and geography. You will learn to identify the varying degrees of social closure and ascription that define different societal hierarchies. This understanding provides the necessary baseline for analyzing why some social positions are inherently more advantageous than others in any given structure.

tasks.title: Culture and the Self Comprehensive Exam
tasks.description: Evaluate the student's ability to apply micro-sociological theories to identity formation, cultural transmission, and group dynamics.

tasks.title: Social Capital
tasks.description: This session explores social capital—the resources inherent in social relations that facilitate collective action. You will learn the difference between bonding and bridging social capital and how access to these resources varies by social class. This connects the study of groups to the larger questions of power and inequality that Unit 3 will address.

tasks.title: Social Networks
tasks.description: This session introduces social network analysis and the concept of 'the strength of weak ties' by Mark Granovetter. You will learn how information and opportunities flow through social ties that aren't necessarily close friendships. This changes your perspective on networking from a 'sleazy' activity to a structural necessity for social mobility.

tasks.title: Organizations and Bureaucracy
tasks.description: This session analyzes the characteristics of ideal-typical bureaucracies as defined by Max Weber and the 'McDonaldization' of society. You will understand the efficiency and the 'iron cage' of rationality that governs modern institutions. This is vital for navigating and critiquing the organizations you deal with daily, from universities to corporations.

tasks.title: Primary and Secondary Groups
tasks.description: This session distinguishes between intimate, long-term primary groups and impersonal, goal-oriented secondary groups. You will learn how the shift from Gemeinschaft (community) to Gesellschaft (society) characterizes modern life. This provides the context for understanding where individuals find emotional support versus instrumental resources.

tasks.title: Cultural and Socialization Field Notes
tasks.description: Conduct initial observations or interviews to identify the core values, norms, and agents of socialization that shape identity within your chosen community.

tasks.title: The Presentation of Self
tasks.description: Using Erving Goffman’s dramaturgical analysis, this session explores the 'front stage' and 'back stage' of social life and the practice of impression management. You will gain a framework for understanding how we perform our identities to others, particularly in the context of social media. This session bridges the gap between individual psychology and social structure.

tasks.title: Roles and Identity
tasks.description: This session defines statuses (ascribed and achieved) and roles, focusing on role conflict and role strain. You will learn how the positions we occupy in society dictate the behaviors expected of us. Mastering these concepts allows you to analyze the structural pressures that cause personal stress in daily life.

tasks.title: Socialization Across the Life Course
tasks.description: This session moves beyond childhood to explore how socialization continues through adolescence, adulthood, and old age. You will examine the concept of 'anticipatory socialization' and 'resocialization' in total institutions. This helps you realize that the 'self' is not a finished product but a continuous social project.

tasks.title: Agents of Socialization
tasks.description: This session identifies the primary groups and institutions—family, school, peers, and mass media—that transmit culture to the individual. You will learn how these agents often provide conflicting messages and how they shape our initial worldviews. Understanding these agents is essential for mapping the 'sociological autobiography' of your own life.

tasks.title: Cultural Capital and Change
tasks.description: This session introduces Pierre Bourdieu's concept of cultural capital and the processes of cultural lag and diffusion. You will understand how cultural knowledge can function as a form of currency that reinforces social class and how technology drives rapid cultural shifts. This links cultural themes to the broader structures of inequality that will be explored in the next unit.

tasks.title: Subcultures and Countercultures
tasks.description: This session distinguishes between subcultures, which exist within the dominant culture, and countercultures, which actively reject it. You will learn to identify the social functions of these groups and how they contribute to social diversity or conflict. This allows you to look past a monolithic view of 'society' and see the vibrant, often conflicting layers of group life.

tasks.title: Symbols and Language
tasks.description: This session examines language as the primary vehicle of culture and the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, which suggests language shapes our perception of reality. You will understand how symbols carry shared meanings and how linguistic shifts reflect social change. This is critical for recognizing how our very thoughts are structured by the cultural tools available to us.

tasks.title: Norms and Values
tasks.description: This session introduces the distinction between values—the abstract ideals of a society—and norms—the specific rules of conduct that implement those values. You will learn to identify folkways, mores, and taboos, gaining the ability to analyze how social order is maintained through informal and formal sanctions. This builds the foundational vocabulary needed to understand why people conform to social expectations in their daily lives.

tasks.title: The Sociological Perspective Comprehensive Exam
tasks.description: Verify the learner's ability to apply the sociological imagination, distinguish between major theoretical paradigms, and evaluate the appropriateness of various research methods for specific social questions.

tasks.title: Research Question and Methodology Design
tasks.description: Define a specific social group or community to study and select the appropriate research methods (ethnography, survey, or interview) to investigate a specific social phenomenon within that group.

tasks.title: Measurement, Causality, and Ethics
tasks.description: This session covers the rigorous requirements of research: operationalizing variables, distinguishing correlation from causation, and adhering to institutional review board (IRB) ethics. You will learn why sociologists must protect human subjects and avoid harm. This ensures you understand sociology not just as a set of ideas, but as an ethical and disciplined science.

tasks.title: Ethnography and Interviews
tasks.description: You will learn about qualitative methods like ethnography (participant observation) and in-depth interviews, which prioritize 'thick description' and the participant's point of view. You will understand how these methods uncover the 'why' behind social patterns. This session emphasizes the 'human' side of data collection often missing from statistics.

tasks.title: Experiments and Field Research
tasks.description: This session compares the controlled environment of laboratory experiments with the naturalistic setting of field research. You will learn how sociologists test hypotheses and observe social behavior in real-time. This helps you understand the trade-offs between 'control' and 'authenticity' in social science.

tasks.title: Surveys and Sampling
tasks.description: You will learn the mechanics of quantitative research, specifically how to design surveys and select representative samples from populations. You will understand why random sampling is necessary to generalize results to a larger group. This knowledge is fundamental for becoming a critical consumer of social statistics and media reports.

tasks.title: Contemporary Theories
tasks.description: This session introduces modern developments such as Feminist Theory and Postmodernism, which challenge and expand traditional perspectives. You will learn how these theories address modern complexities like intersectionality and the decline of 'grand narratives.' This ensures your sociological master-toolkit is up-to-date for contemporary social issues.

tasks.title: Symbolic Interactionism
tasks.description: You will explore the micro-level perspective of symbolic interactionism, focusing on how individuals create meaning through social interaction. You will learn how symbols—words, gestures, and objects—shape our shared reality. This session transitions the course toward the study of the self and identity in Unit 2.

tasks.title: Conflict Theory
tasks.description: This session covers the conflict perspective, rooted in the work of Karl Marx, which focuses on power, inequality, and social struggle. You will learn how social structures often benefit some groups at the expense of others. This is a crucial foundation for Unit 3, where we will dive deeper into racial and gender-based inequality.

tasks.title: Functionalism
tasks.description: You will examine the functionalist perspective, which views society as a complex system of interrelated parts working together to promote solidarity and stability. You will learn about manifest and latent functions, as well as social dysfunctions. This helps you understand the 'macro' logic of how social order is maintained across time.

tasks.title: Sociology and Everyday Life
tasks.description: This session applies the sociological perspective to mundane activities, showing how even the most private acts are socially patterned. You will learn to 'make the familiar strange' by questioning things you usually take for granted. This develops your ability to conduct applied analysis on your own daily routines, a core skill for the later units on culture and institutions.

tasks.title: Social Facts
tasks.description: This session introduces Émile Durkheim’s 'social facts,' which are ways of acting and thinking external to the individual that exert social control. You will learn to identify these invisible forces, such as laws, morals, and customs, that shape collective behavior. This helps you develop the critical awareness needed to see society as a distinct reality worthy of scientific study.

tasks.title: Structure and Agency
tasks.description: This session explores the tension between agency—your power to act independently—and social structure—the organized patterns of relationships that limit your choices. You will understand how society both constrains and enables human action. Mastering this balance is key to moving beyond a purely individualistic worldview toward a sophisticated sociological analysis.

tasks.title: The Sociological Imagination
tasks.description: In this session, you will learn C. Wright Mills' concept of the 'sociological imagination,' which distinguishes between 'personal troubles' and 'public issues.' By the end, you will be able to connect your private biography with historical and social structures. This foundational concept is essential for your course project, as it provides the lens through which you will analyze your own life path.
